q: Standard rebar lengths
n: Reinforcing bars in the Philippines are supplied in standard commercial lengths of 6.0, 7.5, 9.0, 10.5 and 12.0 m. Source: PNS 49:2002 (Steel Bars for Concrete Reinforcement); Max Fajardo, Simplified Construction Estimate.

q: What is used to support steel rebars in the formwork of a reinforced concrete beam?
n: A bolster is a continuous wire bar support that holds rebars at the correct height and cover inside beam and slab forms. Source: CRSI Manual of Standard Practice (Bar Supports); ACI 315.

q: A Class A concrete mixture is
n: The Class A mix is 1:2:4 (cement : sand : gravel), giving about 3,000 psi (21 MPa). Class AA is 1:1.5:3, Class B 1:2.5:5, and Class C 1:3:6. Source: Max Fajardo, Simplified Construction Estimate (Concrete Proportion); DPWH Standard Specifications, Item 405.

q: When is the most important period of curing concrete for it to improve strength and durability?
n: The first 7 days are the most critical for curing. Hydration and strength gain are fastest then, and early drying causes plastic shrinkage cracks and permanent strength loss. Source: ACI 308R (Guide to External Curing of Concrete); Kosmatka et al., Design and Control of Concrete Mixtures (PCA), Ch. 12.

q: A contractor in Manila is casting multiple reinforced concrete columns during peak summer conditions, where daytime temperatures regularly exceed 33°C and humidity remains high. The project follows a fast-track schedule, requiring the same set of steel column forms to be reused for the next level as soon as safely possible. The concrete mix uses ordinary Portland cement, no early loads will be applied, and the elevated summer heat accelerates initial hydration. Under these conditions, when is it most appropriate to strip the column formwork?
n: Vertical forms of columns and walls carry no load and may be stripped after 1–2 days. In hot weather with ordinary Portland cement, about 24 hours is enough. Source: ACI 347R (Guide to Formwork for Concrete), Sec. 3.7 (Removal of Forms); NSCP 2015, Sec. 426.

q: Which cement is best suited for places susceptible to chloride or sulfate attack, such as substructures, bored piles and marine structures, and for water-retaining structures such as retaining walls, ports and tunnels, for improved impermeability? It continues to gain strength after the 28-day period and is known to double its strength over 10 to 12 years.
n: Portland blast-furnace slag cement (GGBFS) resists chloride and sulfate attack and has low permeability. It keeps gaining strength well beyond 28 days, which suits piles, marine works and water-retaining structures. Source: ASTM C595 (Blended Hydraulic Cements); ACI 233R (Slag Cement in Concrete).

q: What filler is used at slab-on-grade construction joints?
n: Construction and isolation joints in slabs on grade commonly use premolded bituminous fiber filler. It is compressible, rot-resistant and cheap. Source: ASTM D1751 (Preformed Bituminous Expansion Joint Filler); ACI 302.1R.

q: What is a good replacement for steel rebars on a large area of a slab on grade if ready-mix concrete is used?
n: Welded wire reinforcement (mesh) is the usual replacement for loose rebars in large slab-on-grade pours. It controls shrinkage cracking and is fast to lay. Source: ACI 360R (Design of Slabs-on-Ground); Wire Reinforcement Institute (WRI) manuals.

q: Which of the following is best used at expansion joints?
n: Expansion joints are filled with compressible foam (closed-cell polyethylene backer or joint filler). It takes up movement and supports the sealant above it. Source: ASTM D5249 (Backer Material for Joint Sealants); ACI 504R (Guide to Sealing Joints).

q: During the waterproofing of a below-grade concrete wall, the architect specifies a material that automatically stops water infiltration by swelling when exposed to moisture. The product must be capable of forming a self-sealing barrier because it expands significantly upon hydration, allowing it to fill cracks and construction joints without relying on surface adhesion. Which material best meets this performance requirement?
n: Bentonite clay swells many times its volume when wet. It forms a self-sealing barrier that closes cracks and joints in below-grade walls without relying on adhesion. Source: ACI 515.2R (Guide to Selecting Protective Treatments); Ching, Building Construction Illustrated, Ch. 3 (Foundation Waterproofing).

q: A senior architect overseeing a podium-deck rehabilitation project in a coastal mixed-use development in Pangasinan notices recurring leaks at the expansion joints and planter boxes. The deck is exposed to intense UV radiation, intermittent ponding due to poor slope, and root intrusion from large tropical plants. The structural consultant requires a waterproofing system that can tolerate substrate movement, resist standing water, bond well to concrete, and provide long-term protection under soil backfill. Which waterproofing system is most appropriate for this condition?
n: A reinforced bituminous (modified-bitumen) membrane with a root barrier suits podium decks and planters. It bonds fully to concrete, tolerates movement and standing water, and lasts under soil backfill. Thin cementitious coats crack, and elastomeric coatings are not made for burial. Source: NRCA Roofing Manual – Membrane Roof Systems (vegetative/podium assemblies); ACI 515.2R.

q: A tiled roofing system requires a waterproof layer beneath the roof tiles to prevent water intrusion caused by wind-driven rain and minor tile displacement. Which membrane is most commonly used for this application?
n: Tiled roofs are laid over a bituminous underlay (roofing felt or a modified-bitumen membrane). It sheds wind-driven rain that gets past displaced or lapped tiles. Source: NRCA Roofing Manual – Steep-Slope Roof Systems (Tile Underlayment); BS 5534 (Slating and Tiling).

q: A construction crew is preparing a roof deck for waterproofing. The specification calls for a system whose underside is heated until it liquefies, allowing it to fuse to the concrete substrate and form a continuous waterproof layer. Which waterproofing category does this system belong to?
n: Torch-applied modified-bitumen sheets are heated on the underside until the bitumen melts. They then fuse to the primed concrete deck as a continuous waterproof layer. They belong to the bituminous membrane category. Source: NRCA Roofing Manual – Membrane Roof Systems (Torch-Applied Modified Bitumen); ASTM D6222.

q: A reinforced concrete roof deck is being designed for a low-rise commercial building. To promote positive drainage, prevent prolonged water accumulation, and minimize the risk of ponding that may accelerate waterproofing failure, what is the most appropriate minimum roof deck slope?
n: Flat concrete roof decks are sloped at least about 1:50 (2%, roughly 1–2°) toward the drains so water never ponds for long. Among the choices, 2° is the appropriate minimum. Source: NRCA Roofing Manual (positive drainage, 1/4 in per ft); NSCP 2015, Sec. 206 (Ponding).

q: An architect is evaluating water-ingress issues on the exterior facade of a mid-rise office building in Ortigas. The facade consists of painted reinforced concrete walls with numerous hairline cracks caused by thermal cycling. The building is fully exposed to sun and rain, and the owner wants a waterproofing system that can bridge hairline cracks, resist UV degradation, remain flexible under daily expansion and contraction, and serve as both a protective and decorative coating. No soil backfill, ponding water or tile toppings are involved. Which waterproofing system is most appropriate for this facade application?
n: Elastomeric coatings dry to a thick, rubbery film. It bridges hairline cracks, stays flexible through daily thermal cycling, resists UV, and doubles as the decorative finish on exposed facades. Source: ASTM D6904 (Wind-Driven Rain Resistance); ASTM C1442 (Elastomeric Wall Coatings).

q: You are asked to assess moisture-related deterioration on a mid-rise dormitory in Baguio City. The existing exterior walls are reinforced concrete with elastomeric paint, but the building continues to suffer from recurring hairline cracks, paint delamination, interior condensation, and mold growth during the cold months. The owner wants a long-term solution that reduces thermal movement, minimizes moisture absorption, and protects the concrete from constant fog, rain and temperature swings. Which building envelope strategy best addresses these climate-specific issues?
o: Apply cementitious waterproofing on the exterior wall surface
Install G.I. sheet cladding as a ventilated rainscreen system
Use asphalt-based sealants on all exterior cracks
Increase the thickness of the elastomeric coating on exterior walls
n: A ventilated rainscreen cladding shields the concrete from fog, rain and temperature swings. Its ventilated cavity drains and dries out moisture, which cuts thermal movement, cracking and condensation. More coats of paint or sealant only treat the surface. Source: Straube & Burnett, Building Science for Building Enclosures (Rainscreen Principle); Allen & Iano, Fundamentals of Building Construction, Ch. 19.

q: Which traditional method of connecting timber roof truss members involves overlapping joints secured by fasteners, and is commonly used in small-scale residential construction for its simplicity and ease of assembly?
n: Bolted lap joints overlap truss members and fasten them with through-bolts. They are simple, easy to assemble and common in small residential timber trusses. Source: NSCP 2015, Ch. 6 (Wood – Bolted Connections); Ching, Building Construction Illustrated, Ch. 6.

q: Minimum roof pitch for a tiled roof
n: Interlocking roof tiles are usually laid at a minimum pitch of about 15° (about 27%). Flatter pitches let wind-driven rain back up past the laps. Source: BS 5534 (Slating and Tiling – minimum pitch tables); concrete tile manufacturers' installation guides.

q: Which roofing system would require the strongest structural support due to its weight and maintenance activity?
n: Clay tile is the heaviest of the listed roofings, at roughly 50–90 kg/sqm. Its framing must carry that dead load and the foot traffic of maintenance crews, so it needs the strongest supports. Metal, shingles and polycarbonate are light. Source: NSCP 2015, Table 204-2 (Minimum Design Dead Loads – Roof Coverings).

q: Which among the choices is the most expensive roofing?
n: Copper costs the most of the listed roofings, both as material and in skilled installation, though it can last a century. Slate and terra cotta come next. Aluminum is cheaper. Source: RSMeans Building Construction Cost Data (Roofing); NRCA Roofing Manual.

q: Recommended thickness for shower glass enclosures
n: Frameless shower enclosures commonly use 10 mm fully tempered glass. It is rigid enough to stand on hinges and clamps without a frame. 8 mm is the lighter, semi-frameless option and 12 mm is for very large panels. Source: GANA Glazing Manual (Shower Enclosures); ANSI Z97.1 (Safety Glazing).

q: Glass recommended for a bathtub enclosure
n: Glazing at bathtubs and showers is a hazardous location that requires safety glazing. Tempered glass breaks into small, blunt pieces and is the standard choice there. Source: ANSI Z97.1 / CPSC 16 CFR 1201 (Safety Glazing in Hazardous Locations); GANA Glazing Manual.

q: Architectural glazing systems enhance both aesthetics and functionality by regulating light transmission, glare and solar gain. Certain glass types use surface-applied coatings that diffuse light while maintaining transparency, reducing discomfort caused by excessive brightness. Which of the following is a specialized glass solution that features ceramic-based coatings fused onto its surface to improve glare control and solar management?
n: Fritted glass has ceramic frit (enamel) patterns fused onto its surface during tempering. The frit diffuses light and cuts glare and solar gain while keeping some transparency. Source: GANA Glazing Manual (Decorative and Ceramic-Frit Glass); Allen & Iano, Fundamentals of Building Construction, Ch. 17.

q: In tropical climates, and in modern glass-clad buildings in particular, intense sunlight causes both excessive heat buildup and glare, affecting indoor comfort and energy efficiency. Which solution provides the best defense against both issues while maintaining indoor comfort, reducing energy costs and keeping sleek building aesthetics?
n: Reflective (solar-control) glass has a metallic coating that reflects much of the incoming solar heat and visible glare. It keeps the sleek all-glass look without added shading devices, blinds or curtains. Source: GANA Glazing Manual (Solar Control Glass); Lechner, Heating, Cooling, Lighting, Ch. 9.

q: Which glass is not ideal for interior spaces?
n: Low-E glass has a coating that controls radiant heat transfer through the building envelope. Inside a building there is no solar or thermal exchange to manage, so it brings no benefit there. Source: GANA Glazing Manual (Low-Emissivity Coatings); Lechner, Heating, Cooling, Lighting.

q: A luxury electric-vehicle showroom is designed with a dramatic cantilevered steel canopy that extends over a frameless glass facade. The architect wants the glass panels to appear as if they are floating, with no visible mullions, while still being securely connected to the structural steel arms supporting the canopy. The connection system must allow point-supported glazing, accommodate slight building movements, and maintain a clean, high-end aesthetic. Which hardware best meets these requirements?
n: Spider fittings are cast stainless-steel arms that hold glass at bolted points with articulated (rotating) bolts. They give the frameless "floating" facade look and allow for building movement. Source: GANA Glazing Manual (Point-Supported Glass Systems); Allen & Iano, Fundamentals of Building Construction, Ch. 17.

q: Which of the following is specifically designed for point-fixed glass assemblies, often used in curtain walls and facades to connect glass panels with minimal framing?
n: Spider fittings are made specifically for point-fixed glass assemblies. Their bolted arms connect glass panels in curtain walls and facades with minimal framing. Patch fittings clamp glass doors, and U-channels frame panel edges. Source: GANA Glazing Manual (Point-Supported Glass Systems).

q: What do you call the putty or glazing compound formed on the exterior side of a glass pane?
n: Face glazing is the putty or glazing compound beveled on the exterior side of the pane after it is set. Bed (back) glazing is the compound laid under the glass. Source: Harris, Dictionary of Architecture and Construction (Face Glazing); Ching, A Visual Dictionary of Architecture.

q: Best material for the walls of a warehouse
n: CHB walls are cheap, quick to build, fire-resistive and tough against impact. That is why they are the usual wall for warehouses. Gypsum is easily damaged, and cast concrete or steel cladding costs more. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated, Ch. 5 (Masonry Walls); Time-Saver Standards for Building Types (Warehouses).

q: Among the following floor options, which is generally the most cost-effective in terms of initial material cost, installation expense and long-term maintenance costs?
n: Ceramic tile has a low material and installation cost and lasts long with little upkeep, so it is the most cost-effective overall. Wood needs refinishing, plastic wears out, and terrazzo costs more to install. Source: RSMeans Building Construction Cost Data (Flooring); Ching, Building Construction Illustrated, Ch. 10.

q: Which of the following flooring materials is considered the most resilient due to its high resistance to moisture, scratches and dents, making it ideal for high-traffic and wet areas?
n: Vinyl is a resilient flooring that resists moisture, scratches and dents and is easy to clean. It suits high-traffic and wet areas better than cork, linoleum or bamboo, which absorb water. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated, Ch. 10 (Resilient Flooring); ASTM F1700 (Vinyl Tile).

q: How do you order engineered wood floorings?
n: Engineered wood flooring is sold in boxes (cartons). Each box holds a stated coverage in square meters, so the floor area is divided by the coverage per box, plus allowance for waste. Source: National Wood Flooring Association (NWFA) Installation Guidelines; manufacturers' packaging data.

q: In construction, finishing materials must balance both functionality and aesthetics, ensuring a seamless transition while protecting surfaces from wear and tear. Although several components contribute to floor integrity, one stands out for its ability to reinforce durability in high-traffic zones while maintaining an attractive appearance. Which option offers the best combination of practicality and visual refinement at surface junctions?
n: A threshold (transition) strip covers the joint where two floorings meet, for example at doorways. It protects the edges from wear in high-traffic zones and gives a neat finish. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated, Ch. 10 (Flooring Transitions); Harris, Dictionary of Architecture and Construction.

q: Door used for large storage areas
n: Roll-up (rolling) doors coil above the opening. They can close very wide openings without taking up interior space, so they are used for warehouses and large storage areas. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated, Ch. 8 (Special Doors); Time-Saver Standards for Building Types.

q: A type of door that can accommodate a large number of people simultaneously
n: A revolving door lets people enter and exit at the same time in a continuous flow. It also keeps out drafts, so it suits busy entrances. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated, Ch. 8 (Revolving Doors); NFPA 101, Sec. 7.2.1.10.

q: A door suitable for getting the best view of a vista, which can span wide lengths
n: Sliding glass doors run on tracks and can span wide openings with large panes. They give an unobstructed view of a vista and take no swing space. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated, Ch. 8 (Sliding Doors).

q: A horizontal bar device that spans the interior of an emergency door
n: Panic hardware is a horizontal bar across the inside of an exit door that releases the latch when pushed. It is required on assembly and other high-occupancy exits. Source: RA 9514 (Fire Code) 2019 RIRR, Div. 10.2.5 (Panic Hardware); NFPA 101, Sec. 7.2.1.7.

q: Which of the following is primarily composed of organic cellulose fibers?
n: Wood is made mainly of cellulose fibers bound by lignin, so it is primarily organic cellulose. Fiber cement board has some cellulose reinforcement, but its main component is Portland cement. Source: USDA Forest Products Laboratory, Wood Handbook, Ch. 2 (Structure and Function of Wood); ASTM C1186 (Fiber-Cement Sheets).

q: Which material is used for top rails that is easy to maintain?
n: Stainless steel railings resist corrosion and need no painting or refinishing. Mild steel rusts, wood needs varnishing, and brass tarnishes. Source: International Stainless Steel Forum (ISSF), Stainless Steel in Architecture; Ching, Building Construction Illustrated, Ch. 9.

q: Stainless steel best used for outdoor railing
n: Grade 316 stainless contains molybdenum and resists chlorides much better than 304. It is the grade specified for outdoor and coastal railings. Source: ASTM A240 (Stainless Steel Plate and Sheet); ISSF, Stainless Steel in Architecture.

q: Stainless steel best used for indoor railing
n: Grade 304 is the standard, economical stainless steel. It resists corrosion well enough for indoor railings and fixtures; 316 is reserved for harsher exterior or coastal exposure. Source: ASTM A240; ISSF, Stainless Steel in Architecture.

q: A popular steel used for indoor railings that has low corrosion resistance
n: Plain carbon (mild) steel has low corrosion resistance and must be painted or powder-coated. Because it is cheap and easy to work, it is still popular for indoor railings. 304 and 316 are stainless. Source: Allen & Iano, Fundamentals of Building Construction, Ch. 11 (Steel); ASTM A36.

q: Which of the following is not a characteristic of aluminum?
n: Aluminum is a good heat conductor and lasts long without emitting VOCs. Being thin and light, it is a poor acoustic insulator. Source: The Aluminum Association, Aluminum Design Manual; Egan, Architectural Acoustics (mass law).

q: Which of the following acoustic materials is generally the lightest in weight while providing effective sound absorption?
n: Open-cell acoustic foam is the lightest of the listed absorbers, at roughly 20–30 kg/m³. Rock wool and fiberglass batts are denser, and cementitious panels are much heavier. Source: Egan, Architectural Acoustics (Porous Absorbers); manufacturer density data.

q: Which would you recommend as insulation for steel columns?
n: Spray-applied fire-resistive material (SFRM), a cementitious or mineral-fiber spray, is the usual insulation that protects steel columns from fire for the required rating. Rigid and spray foams are combustible. Source: RA 9514 (Fire Code) RIRR (fire-resistive construction); UL Fire Resistance Directory; ASTM E119.

q: Which of the following is most suited for use as a pile?
n: Of the choices, Apitong is the strong, heavy structural hardwood used for piles and heavy construction. Kamagong is a cabinet wood, lauan is light, and narra is for furniture. Ipil, yakal and molave would be better still. Source: DENR-FPRDI, Philippine Woods (Uses of Apitong); NSCP 2015, Ch. 6 (Wood).

q: Lumber is sold in units of
n: Lumber is sold in even-foot lengths, such as 8, 10, 12 and 14 ft. Source: Max Fajardo, Simplified Construction Estimate (Lumber); American Softwood Lumber Standard PS 20.

q: This wood joint is created by cutting a groove along one edge of a board, while on the other edge a centered extension is formed to fit into the corresponding groove of another piece. Except for the end piece, all boards using this joint have both components cut into their edges. It is used to make edge-to-edge joints for wide panels, floorings, sidings, wall paneling, ceilings, shelving edges, and cabinet and furniture sides, but its most common use is for wood floorings.
n: A tongue-and-groove joint has a centered tongue on one edge that fits a groove on the next board. It makes flush edge-to-edge panels and is used most for wood flooring. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated, Ch. 10 (Wood Flooring); Spence, Carpentry and Building Construction (Joinery).

q: A foreman is assembling a wooden frame that must remain strong and dimensionally stable over time. To prevent twisting, racking and warping caused by seasonal wood movement, which type of joint should be used to achieve the strongest and most warp-resistant connection?
n: A mortise-and-tenon joint locks the members together on several faces with a large glue area. It resists twisting, racking and warping better than lap, butt or most other joints, so it is used for frames. Source: Spence, Carpentry and Building Construction (Joinery); Hoadley, Understanding Wood.
